records.text: Woo, a fork! One piece is threatening a whole bunch of targets in the very same move, and that's so much fun to see.
Oh boy, trouble: the other side now has a fork. One of their pieces could jump at several targets in one go. Little lesson: count which squares hit two things at once.
Oh, so close! A different move had a fork, one piece jumping at several targets together. This move zooms right past it, but we can learn it now.
Wow, pinned against the king! That piece is stuck where it stands, because moving would leave its king wide open.
Uh oh, heads up! The other side can pin a piece against its king now, and then it has to stay frozen on that line.
Aw, nearly! Another move had a pin waiting, and that piece would have been frozen right in front of its king. This move lets the chance go.
Yes, a skewer! The front piece is under attack, and when it scoots away, the piece behind it gets hit on the same line.
Yikes, two pieces are standing in a row, and the other side can skewer them. If the front one hops away, the back one could get hit.
Ooh, one got away! A different move set up a skewer: nudge the front piece off the line, and the piece behind would have been the one to fall. Let's remember that line.
Gotcha! First the defender gets captured, and now the piece it was protecting has nobody looking after it.
Eek, a defender is up for capture now. Lose it, and whatever it was protecting is left without a guard.
Oopsie, a missed chance! With another move, a defender would have been knocked out, its job left undone. This move skips that trick.
Hooray, back-rank alert! The king is penned in by its own pieces, and this move heads straight there.
Oh boy, the king's own pieces are crowding its exits. That opens the door to a back-rank mate for the other side.
Oh, so close! A back-rank mate was sitting there, with the king penned in by its own pieces. This move went a different way.
Go, little pawn, go! Zooming up the board, and once it lands on the last rank, it turns into a whole new piece.
Uh oh, one of their pawns can run for the last rank now. Promotion could be coming for the other side.
Aw, nearly! A stronger move opened a road for a pawn to promote. This move leaves the pawn's path shut.
Yippee! One piece hops out of the way, and boom, the hidden piece springs into action. That's what a discovered attack looks like!
Yikes, a piece of theirs is parked in front of another. If it hops aside, the one behind gets to attack. Watch for that discovered attack!
Ooh, one got away! A different move had a discovered attack, one piece hopping aside so the one behind could pounce. This move keeps it hidden.
Woo, double trouble! One move, and out come two threats, and both of them want an answer.
Eek, two threats from a single move are now available to the other side. Answering both is the hard part.
Oopsie, a missed chance! A stronger move made two threats at the same time. That double attack slips away this time.
Nailed it! The defender gets tugged off its job, and the spot it was covering is wide open now. That's a deflection, and a sneaky-smart one!
Oh boy, that defender is working hard, and the other side can tug it off its job. A deflection like that leaves its spot uncovered.
Oh, so close! Another move could have tugged a defender off its job. That deflection waits for another day.
Gotcha! Nobody was looking after that piece, so it gets gobbled up. Easy points!
Aw, nearly! Another move could have gobbled up a piece with no guard at all. This move trots right past it. Easy habit: look for anything unguarded before you move.
Uh oh, a piece has no guard now, and nothing stops the other side from gobbling it up.
Ah, found the problem! That piece only had one real defender, and this move sends it away, so the other side can capture. Quick tip: before a defender leaves, see what it was guarding.
Whoops! A threat came with the opponent's last move, and since this move ignores it, a piece can be captured. Little lesson: start by asking what their last move threatens.
Hmm, that first capture sure looks yummy, but then the other side recaptures, and what it grabs back is worth more. Easy habit: count every capture in the swap, both sides.
A minor piece hops out of its starting spot and joins the team!
Another move would have developed a minor piece, bringing it out of its starting spot.
The rook found an open file, without a single pawn of either color on it. Zoom zoom!
A different move would have handed a rook an open file, totally free of pawns.
The rook steps onto a semi-open file: none of its own pawns are there, but at least one enemy pawn still is.
Ooh, a semi-open file was there for a rook with another move, empty of its own pawns while an enemy pawn still sits on it.
Ooh, a passed pawn! No enemy pawn blocks its way, on its file or either file next door.
A different move would have made a passed pawn, with no enemy pawn blocking its way on its file or either file next door.

Hmm, nothing is guarding this piece now. Good to notice, even though unguarded doesn't mean it can be won.

The king gets a brand-new spot it's legally allowed to step on. More wiggle room!
With a different move, the king would have gained a new legal spot to step on.

Another choice was castling, so king and rook both move in a single turn.

With another move, two same-colored pawns would have stacked up on one file.
